source.title: MiniPLM: Knowledge Distillation for Pre-Training Language Models
source.authors: Yu-Xian Gu; Hao Zhou; Fan-Dong Meng; Jie Zhou; Minlie Huang

record.tranche_reason: The paper fits held-out language-model loss as a function of training compute and reports downstream performance across student sizes in a knowledge-distillation setting. This bears on scaling behavior, but it does not reproduce the original broad parameter/token/compute sweeps.
record.gate_note: The study fits test-loss curves and reports downstream accuracy across model sizes. Its 1T and 10T loss values are predictions from fitted curves, not evaluations of runs at those scales. It cites scaling-law results as motivation and as the basis for extrapolation; cited results are not recorded as rows.
record.test_reason: This is a knowledge-distillation method paper. It uses the Hoffmann et al. loss form as a tool: it fits L(C)=L∞+Ac/C^αc to each method's DCLM test-loss curve over less than about 1.5 orders of magnitude of compute (about 0.1–3.5×10^20 FLOPs). It then extrapolates to 1T and 10T tokens to argue that MiniPLM's advantage persists. It reports no fit quality, no held-out check of the fit, and no test of whether the power law holds. The downstream rows compare MiniPLM with Vanilla KD, i.e. its own method against baselines. They do not test whether downstream performance is predictable from scale or loss.
record.authors_conclusion: Essentially correct. The authors conclude that MiniPLM improves downstream accuracy and DCLM loss and reduces pretraining compute (2.2× vs Vanilla KD for 500M). They also conclude it enables cross-family KD and cuts data needs by 2.4× in the data-limited setting. Its advantage at 1T/10T tokens rests only on scaling-law extrapolation, not on observed runs.
record.recipe_differences: Measures held-out loss versus training compute for fixed student sizes and fits a compute-scaling formula, rather than testing the original broad parameter, token, and compute sweeps. The large-token losses are extrapolations, not observed runs.
record.method_sensitivity: The fitted compute exponent varies by student size and training method.

fits_no_version.finding: Fitted compute exponents αc on single-size training-loss curves range 0.41–0.59 depending on the KD method or data distribution (Table 10). The fits have no uncertainty and span a narrow compute range.
fits_no_version.proposed_claim: Altering the pretraining data distribution (e.g. teacher-guided data selection) changes the fitted loss-vs-compute exponent for a fixed model size.

record.problems: The loss curves are shown in figures, and the paper does not provide fit-quality statistics or uncertainty for the fitted parameters. The 1T and 10T losses are extrapolated rather than verified on runs at those scales. The tested compute fits do not establish parameter- or token-scaling laws independently.
record.rows_left_out: Figure 1 and Appendix Figure 7 contain downstream-accuracy scaling curves, and Figure 4 contains the detailed loss curves. Their pointwise values are figure-only; the reported fitted parameters and the cross-size average accuracies in Table 5 were retained instead.

untested.parts: Not tested. The power-law form is assumed and fitted to short training curves without assessing fit.
Extrapolations to 1T/10T tokens (Table 2) are never checked against real runs.
Data-constrained extrapolation (Muennighoff law) is used as a tool, not tested.
No predictive relation between scale or loss and downstream accuracy is fitted or tested.
Exponents differ by method, but without uncertainty or fit diagnostics. The variation is not analysed as fit dependence.

record.verdict_notes: Downgraded from tests/T2 to uses_without_test/T4. All reader labels (V1, V6, V7 supports) are removed. Table 10 lists C10T equal to C1T for the 500M and 1.2B rows (3.14×10^21, 7.30×10^21), apparently a typo. Eq. (16) collapses the Chinchilla form to compute at fixed size, setting αc=αd.

versions.untested_parts: Tests loss scaling with training compute at fixed student sizes. Does not separately test scaling with parameter count or training tokens while the other quantities are not bottlenecks, or establish the claim over several orders of magnitude.
The paper predicts losses at 1T and 10T tokens using fits to smaller runs, but does not compare those predictions with runs actually trained at those scales.
No compute-optimal parameter/token allocation sweep or fitted allocation trend.
No controlled comparison of depth, width, or other architecture details at fixed parameter count.
The study is about text pre-training and does not test other modalities, repeated-data scaling laws as a general law, or fine-tuning and transfer scaling.
Reports downstream accuracy by student size and method, but does not fit or validate a general predictive relationship between downstream results and pre-training loss.

Reports fitted compute exponents across different model sizes and training methods. Does not compare parameter-counting or fitting procedures, establish disagreement between the original sources, test compute-optimal allocations, or report curves bending away from a power law.

rows.subject: Qwen 200M student LM
rows.operation_detail: Fit test loss as a function of training compute using Eq. (16), L(C) = L∞ + Ac/C^αc.
rows.measure: Fitted test-loss scaling parameters L∞, Ac, and αc
rows.locator: Appendix D.2, Table 10; fit uses Figure 4
rows.note: The paper fits this power-law form to the plotted loss-versus-compute curve; it does not report a fit-quality statistic.
rows.check: Fitted constants used as a tool to extrapolate a method comparison. No fit-quality statistic, compute span under two orders of magnitude, no validation. Cannot show whether a power law holds (V1) or what drives exponent differences (V7).

reader_labels.label: supports
reader_labels.condition: Reported test-loss-versus-compute fits for 200M, 500M, and 1.2B students across the three training methods
reader_labels.reason: The study fits a decreasing power-law compute term to each loss curve; see r1–r9. The evidence covers compute scaling at fixed sizes only.

reader_labels.label: supports
reader_labels.condition: MiniPLM Qwen student models at 200M, 500M, and 1.2B parameters
reader_labels.reason: The reported average downstream accuracy rises across the tested student sizes from 41.3% to 44.8% to 46.6%; see r11, r13, and r15.

reader_labels.label: supports
reader_labels.condition: Fitted compute exponents across student sizes and training methods
reader_labels.reason: The fitted αc values vary across the reported methods and sizes, from 0.41 to 0.59; see r1–r9. The paper does not test the other parts of V7.
